planting.note: Start seeds indoors in late summer for fall transplanting where foxglove is grown as a winter annual or biennial, or sow in very early spring under lights 10-12 weeks before the last frost for first-year bloom farther north. Camelot Rose is part of the Camelot series, an All-America Selections winning foxglove strain bred for reliable first-year flowering and improved heat tolerance compared to older heirloom foxglove strains.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil. Camelot Rose bears dense, upright spikes of large, outward-facing, rose-pink bells with heavy maroon speckling deep in the throat, opening the first year from an early sowing rather than requiring the traditional two-year biennial wait. Its sturdy, well-branched stems hold up well without staking in most garden sites, and its improved heat tolerance relative to older foxglove strains makes it a dependable choice through warm summers. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas frequented by children or pets and wear gloves when handling the foliage.
sources: All-America Selections — Digitalis Camelot series notes
University of Georgia Extension — Digitalis purpurea as a Southern Biennial

common_name: Camelot Lavender Foxglove (Soft Lavender-Purple First-Year-Blooming Foxglove)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors in late summer for fall transplanting where foxglove is grown as a winter annual or biennial, or sow in very early spring under lights 10-12 weeks before the last frost for first-year bloom farther north. Camelot Lavender is part of the Camelot series, an All-America Selections winning foxglove strain bred for reliable first-year flowering and improved heat tolerance compared to older heirloom foxglove strains.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil. Camelot Lavender produces tall, densely packed spikes of soft lavender-purple, outward-facing bells with a paler throat marked in fine maroon speckling, opening the first year from an early sowing rather than requiring the traditional two-year biennial wait. The sturdy, well-branched habit resists flopping in wind and rain better than many older foxglove strains, making it useful for mixed borders and large containers as well as traditional cottage-garden plantings. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas frequented by children or pets and wear gloves when handling the foliage.
sources: All-America Selections — Digitalis Camelot series notes
University of Georgia Extension — Digitalis purpurea as a Southern Biennial

common_name: Dalmatian Peach Foxglove (Compact First-Year-Blooming Peach Foxglove)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, since the Dalmatian series needs a longer head start than some foxglove strains to reliably flower the first year; transplant out after frost danger has passed into partial shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil, and keep evenly moist through establishment since this compact series has a shallower root system than taller heirloom foxglove strains. Dalmatian Peach is a named color selection within the dwarf, vegetatively uniform Dalmatian series, bred for landscape beds and containers, topping out under two feet with densely packed spikes of speckled, tubular bells in a soft peach-apricot shade. Its compact, self-supporting habit needs no staking and fits smaller garden spaces and mixed containers better than the taller old-fashioned biennial types. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic if ingested, so plant away from areas frequented by children or pets.
sources: PanAmerican Seed / Danziger — Dalmatian foxglove series notes

common_name: Illumination Raspberry Digiplexis (Raspberry-Pink Repeat-Flowering Foxglove Hybrid)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Illumination Raspberry is a sterile intergeneric hybrid grown from cuttings, not seed, and it flowers continuously without needing deadheading for seed removal.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, providing afternoon shade and consistent moisture where summers are hottest. Illumination Raspberry is part of the Digiplexis group, a race of sterile intergeneric hybrids between common foxglove (Digitalis purpurea) and the Canary Island shrub foxglove (Isoplexis canariensis), combining the tall spike form of foxglove with a shrubbier, longer-lived, repeat-flowering habit; its tubular flowers open in rich raspberry-pink with a deeper throat, distinct from the flame-orange tones of the original Illumination Flame. Because the plant is sterile, it channels its energy into producing new flowering spikes all season instead of setting seed. It behaves as a short-lived tender perennial, reliably overwintering outdoors only in the mildest zones, but performs as a long-blooming summer annual almost everywhere else. Deadhead spent spikes to the base to encourage fresh flowering stems, and note that, like other foxgloves, all parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall for winter and spring bloom; ranunculus corms must be pre-soaked 3-4 hours in cool water before planting to rehydrate the dry corms. Plant with the claw-like corm facing downward, 2 inches deep. The Tecolote series is one of the premier commercial ranunculus series in the world, bred in the Carpinteria, California area, one of the world's major ranunculus production centers.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist soil; ranunculus requires excellent drainage, especially in winter, since wet soil causes corm rot. Tecolote Orange is a named color selection in the Tecolote Series, producing large, fully double, multi-petaled flowers in a vivid, warm orange that provides a bright accent among the cooler pinks, reds, and whites of other Tecolote colors. The flowers are composed of densely packed, tissue-thin petals in concentric rings that create a structure resembling a perfectly formed, layered rose, making Tecolote ranunculus a premium choice for high-end cut flower production and upscale spring garden display. The corms cannot tolerate summer heat; dig and store in a cool, dry location after foliage yellows, or treat as an annual and replace each fall.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Ranunculus asiaticus Tecolote Series Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Ranunculus for Florida Cut Flower Production

planting.note: Plant corms in fall for winter and spring bloom; ranunculus corms must be pre-soaked 3-4 hours in cool water before planting to rehydrate the dry corms. Plant with the claw-like corm facing downward, 2 inches deep. The Tecolote series is one of the premier commercial ranunculus series in the world, bred in the Carpinteria, California area, one of the world's major ranunculus production centers.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist soil; ranunculus requires excellent drainage, especially in winter, since wet soil causes corm rot. Tecolote Pink is a named color selection in the Tecolote Series, producing large, fully double, multi-petaled flowers in a clear, soft pink with the extraordinary petal density and precision of form that makes Tecolote ranunculus the premium choice for high-end cut flower production and upscale spring garden display. In zone 9, planted in fall for February-April bloom, it provides a spectacular spring floral display during the late-winter window when few other garden plants flower at this level of quality. The corms cannot tolerate summer heat; dig and store in a cool, dry location after foliage yellows, or treat as an annual and replace each fall.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Ranunculus asiaticus Tecolote Series Production

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike the wild species, the fully double 'Flore Pleno' sets little or no viable seed, so it does not self-sow into a weedy colony, though it still spreads by rooting stolons and should be given a contained bed or edged border away from lawns and wild areas.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping buttercup thrives in damp ground that would rot most other border perennials, making it useful along pond margins, rain gardens, and moist shaded banks. 'Flore Pleno' bears fully double, bright golden-yellow pompom flowers over glossy, three-lobed foliage from late spring into summer, a much showier and better-behaved alternative to the plain-flowered wild species, which is a notoriously aggressive lawn and garden weed in damp soil. Because the double flowers rarely set seed, this cultivar spreads only by its rooting stolons rather than by scattering seed into surrounding beds, but it still forms a dense, vigorous mat over time and should be sited where its spread is welcome or contained by an edging barrier. Divide congested patches in spring to control size and share.

common_name: Fair Maids of France (Double White Aconite-Leaf Buttercup)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Fair Maids of France is a long-cultivated cottage-garden heirloom, first recorded in the 16th century, grown for its neat mounds of dark green, deeply lobed foliage topped by wiry, branching stems of small, perfectly double white pompom flowers.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, providing consistent moisture through the growing season since this European woodland-edge species dislikes drying out. Fair Maids of France bears wiry, branching stems set with small, fully double, button-like white flowers over dark green, deeply cut, aconite-like foliage from late spring into early summer, a refined and long-cultivated cottage-garden heirloom quite different in form from the large, ruffled Persian ranunculus grown from corms. It combines well with hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials at the front of a border. Established clumps are long-lived and increase slowly by short rhizomes; divide only when clumps become congested, as plants resent frequent disturbance and settle in best when left undisturbed for several years.

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Atropurpurea Group is the original, longer-grown bronze-purple-leaved seed strain of Actaea simplex, predating named clonal cultivars such as 'Brunette' and 'Hillside Black Beauty', and shows some natural variation in leaf darkness and flower tone from plant to plant since it is propagated from seed rather than division.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Atropurpurea Group is the classic older bugbane strain grown from selected seed for its deeply divided, bronze-purple to purple-brown foliage, a color that deepens through the season and provides months of dark textural contrast in the shade garden before the tall, wand-like flower spikes appear. In late summer and fall, fragrant white to faintly pink-tinged bottlebrush racemes rise 4-6 feet above the foliage, drawing late-season pollinators on the evening air. Because it is a seed strain rather than a single clone, plants show mild variation in leaf darkness and habit compared to named cultivars, but it remains a widely available and reliable choice for large shaded borders. Performs best in zones 3-7 with moderate summers; in zone 8, site in the coolest, most consistently moist position available.
scientific_name_note: Sold both as 'Atropurpurea' and as the Atropurpurea Group seed strain; formerly classified as Cimicifuga simplex Atropurpurea Group.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery stock in spring into deep, fertile, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Elstead is a British Award of Garden Merit-winning selection prized for its dark purple-black stems and buds contrasting against fresh green foliage.

directions: Site in cool, evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the roots from drying out over summer. Elstead carries slender, near-black purple stems and tightly packed purple-tinged flower buds that open to narrow, fragrant white bottlebrush racemes in early to mid fall, one of the darker-stemmed selections among the white-flowered bugbanes and a striking contrast against its clean, fresh-green, finely divided foliage. Established clumps are long-lived and resent transplanting once settled in, so choose the permanent site with care. Pair with hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials for a layered woodland border, and stake in exposed sites since the tall flower spikes can lean in wind.
scientific_name_note: Formerly classified as Cimicifuga simplex 'Elstead' or Cimicifuga matsumurae 'Elstead'.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Award of Garden Merit

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or nursery-grown transplants in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; Mountain Bugbane is native to rich, rocky, mid-to-high-elevation forests of the Appalachians from Pennsylvania to Georgia and flowers later in the season than the related black cohosh.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions or nursery-grown transplants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade. Actaea podocarpa (formerly Cimicifuga americana), commonly called mountain bugbane, is a native Appalachian woodland perennial closely related to black cohosh (Actaea racemosa) but noticeably smaller and later-blooming, sending up slender, branching spikes of small white flowers from late summer into fall, well after A. racemosa has finished. Its rounded, compound leaflets are less coarsely toothed than those of black cohosh, and its distinctly long-stalked seed pods (the source of the species name, meaning 'stalked fruit') distinguish it from its relatives once flowering has finished. It is a fine choice for extending the bloom season in a native shaded woodland garden alongside ferns, hostas, and spring ephemerals; purchase only nursery-propagated stock and never collect from the wild.
